docs.title: apns-push-relay
docs.text:
A generic, self-hostable web API that delivers APNs pushes on behalf of your backends — without giving them your Apple keys, and without letting anyone turn your relay into a spam cannon.

Your backend holds one tenant token and a signing key; the relay holds the .p8 provider keys, verifies every request, enforces quotas, and forwards to Apple. The relay never stores who your users are, what your payloads say, or where their tokens came from.

docs.title: The four moving parts
docs.text:
graph LR
    B[Tenant backend<br/>token + Ed25519 key] -->|signed requests| R[apns-push-relay<br/>quotas · denylist · grants]
    A[iOS app<br/>App Attest + consent] -->|enrollment| R
    R -->|.p8 provider JWTs| P[APNs]
    P -->|push| A
    D[(SQLite<br/>blind indexes only)] -.-> R

  • Privacy by design No device table, no payload storage, no content in logs. Destination tokens exist only as keyed blind indexes. See Privacy.

  • Abuse controls Per-minute and daily quotas, per-token rate limits, denylist, instant revocation, 30-day non-use deletion. See Limits & abuse.

  • Real enrollment Destination-bound grants issued only after App Attest verification, a challenge push, and explicit in-app user consent.

  • Yours to run One docker compose up: nginx + certbot + relay. No hostnames, bundles or quotas are hardcoded — it is all config.yaml. See Self-hosting.

docs.title: Trust panel
docs.text: The relay sees… The relay never sees… Your tenant token digest + public key Your signing private key Destination token blind index (HMAC) Who your users are, device tables Payload sizes, kinds, and results Payload content (sealed blobs opaque) Route, status code, latency (logs) Tokens, grants, or content in logs

docs.title: Limits at a glance
docs.text:
Limit Default (per App, operator-set) Burst burst_per_min per tenant Per-destination burst token_burst_per_min Daily daily per tenant Grant TTL grant_ttl: min..max, default default Idle tenant deletion 30 days without use

Check live numbers on the Status page.

docs.title: Three ways in
docs.text:
1. I run my own backend → Getting started: register, enroll your app's devices, push.
  2. I want to self-host the relay → Self-hosting: compose up in minutes, relay doctor validates everything.
  3. I want to understand it first → How it works: architecture, request flow, and the three push kinds.

MIT licensed · Source · Report abuse · Contact

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This is the tenant path: you run a backend, you want to send pushes to your own app's users through a relay.

docs.title: 1. Register (two variants)
docs.text:
POST /v1/register — unauthenticated, rate-limited per IP. One token per App, forever (or until an operator revokes it).

Plain registrationCallback verification (ownership proof)

Use this when the operator's App config does not require a callback:

curl -sS -X POST https://api.push.example.org/v1/register \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"id": "hooks.example.com", "app": "my-app"}'

{
  "tenant": "hooks.example.com",
  "app": "my-app",
  "token": "tnt_…",
  "quota": {"burst_per_min": 60, "daily": 10000, "token_burst_per_min": 30},
  "registered_at": 1792230900,
  "expires_at": 1794822900
}

The id must be your hostname or a subdomain of it — it is what grants are bound to. Store the token like a password: it is shown once.

Some Apps set registration.callback_required: true. Then your response must include a public HTTPS endpoint the relay will challenge:

{"id": "hooks.example.com", "app": "my-app",
 "callback": "https://hooks.example.com/relay-hook"}

The relay POSTs {"id": …, "kind": "registration", "nonce": …} and requires {"nonce": "<same value>"} back — inline, before the 201.

Requirements (enforced): HTTPS on port 443 only; the callback host must equal your id or a subdomain of it; DNS resolves to a public address only (the callback can never probe private networks).

Errors: invalid_callback (bad URL / host mismatch), callback_verification_failed (no echo), id_exists (already registered — first claim wins).

docs.title: 2. Sign every request
docs.text:
Signed routes — /v1/push, /v1/enroll/renew, /v1/revoke, /v1/rotate — need an Ed25519 keypair. You send the public key at enrollment (tenantPubkey); the private key never leaves your backend.

Canonical message (exact bytes, \n-joined):

SHA256HEX(token) \n METHOD \n PATH \n TIMESTAMP \n NONCE \n SHA256HEX(body)

import base64, hashlib, secrets, time
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey

def sign(private: Ed25519PrivateKey, token: str, method: str, path: str,
         body: bytes, timestamp: int | None = None, nonce: str | None = None):
    ts = str(timestamp or int(time.time()))
    nonce = nonce or secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
    message = "\n".join([
        hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest(),
        method, path, ts, nonce, hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest(),
    ]).encode()
    sig = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(private.sign(message)).decode().rstrip("=")
    return {
        "authorization": f"Bearer {token}",
        "x-relay-time": ts,
        "x-relay-nonce": nonce,
        "x-relay-signature": sig,
    }

Rules: timestamp ±5 minutes; nonces are 8–128 chars, single-use for 10 minutes; sign the raw body bytes you send.

Failures are precise: missing_token, unknown_tenant, enrollment_required, invalid_timestamp, stale_timestamp, invalid_nonce, invalid_signature, replayed_nonce (all 401).

docs.title: 3. Enroll a device (in your app)
docs.text:
Per device, three calls (see the enrollment spec for the full contract):

  1. POST /v1/enroll/begin {app, tenantId, destinationToken} → the relay sends the device a silent challenge push → {challengeId, serverChallenge, expiresAt}.
  2. POST /v1/enroll/finish {challengeId, attestation, assertion, tenantId, tenantPubkey, kinds, ttl?} → {grant, consent}.
  3. Hand the grant to your backend over your existing channel (the relay never contacts you).

ttl is optional and clamped to the App's configured bounds (e.g. 900–86400s; omitted → App default). Renew with POST /v1/enroll/renew before expiry — no re-attestation needed.

docs.title: 4. Push
docs.text:
curl -sS -X POST https://api.push.example.org/v1/push \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "x-relay-time: $TS" -H "x-relay-nonce: $NONCE" -H "x-relay-signature: $SIG" \
  -d '{"grant":"v1.…","destinationToken":"<hex>","kind":"alert",
       "content":{"alert":{"title":"Build finished","body":"all tests green"}}}'

{ "result": "accepted", "apnsId": "8F2A…", "detail": null }

Results are always 200:

result meaning accepted APNs took it (apnsId set) invalidDestination token is dead/unregistered for this app/environment retryable network/APNs hiccup — back off and retry rejected APNs refused (payload/topic/auth) — see detail

Pre-flight failures are not 200: 401 auth codes, 403 grant codes (grant_expired, grant_revoked, grant_mismatch, destination_mismatch, kind_not_allowed, …), 429 (rate_limited, token_rate_limited, quota_exhausted), 422 payload codes (*_too_long, unknown_field, invalid_payload).

docs.title: 5. Revoke
docs.text:
POST /v1/revoke  {"grant": "v1.…"}   → {"revoked": "<jti>"}

The jti is denylisted until its expiry; the next push with that grant fails 403 grant_revoked. Alternatively your operator can kill a whole tenant instantly (relay tenant revoke).

docs.title: 6. Rotate credentials
docs.text:
POST /v1/rotate  {"pubkey": "<new Ed25519 pubkey, base64url>"}   → {"token": "tnt_…", …}

Signed with your current token and keypair — the signature is the proof you hold the binding being rotated. The response replaces both credentials: the new token is shown once, the new pubkey becomes the signing key. Old grants stop verifying (403 tenant_mismatch), so paired devices re-enroll with the new key; sending your current pubkey rotates only the token. See enrollment spec §2.7 for the full semantics.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │                 your host                  │
 tenant backend ───►│ nginx (TLS, rate limit, /admin → 404)      │
   signed HTTP      │   └── uvicorn + FastAPI  (apns-relay)      │
                    │         ├── SQLite WAL (tenants, quotas,   │
                    │         │   nonces, challenges, denylist)  │
                    │         └── APNs sender (.p8 JWTs, http/2) │──► APNs
                    │                                            │
                    │ certbot (ACME, auto-renew)                 │
                    └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • nginx terminates TLS, enforces coarse per-IP rate limits, and never proxies /admin to the app. /docs, /redoc and /openapi.json are proxied but served only by instances that opt in (server.swagger_ui).
  • The relay app authenticates, authorizes, quotas, and forwards.
  • certbot renews certificates on a timer; nginx reloads.
  • SQLite (WAL) holds only blind material: token digests, HMAC'd destination indexes, single-use nonces, challenge hashes, denylist keys.

docs.title: Request flow: a push
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Backend
    participant R as Relay
    participant A as APNs
    B->>R: POST /v1/push (Bearer tnt_…, X-Relay-Time/Nonce/Signature)
    R->>R: token → tenant, Ed25519 verify, nonce single-use
    R->>R: grant verify (sig, exp, denylist, bindings, kind)
    R->>R: payload caps + unknown-field rejection
    R->>R: quotas (tenant burst → per-token burst → daily)
    R->>A: provider JWT + topic/env from config
    A-->>R: 200 + apns-id / 4xx reason
    R-->>B: 200 {"result": "accepted" | "invalidDestination" | "retryable" | "rejected"}

Every push returns HTTP 200 with a machine-readable result; structured pre-flight failures (auth, grant, quota, payload) return their own status codes with stable error strings. See the API reference.

docs.title: The three push kinds
docs.text:
kind APNs push type Priority Topic Use alert alert 10 bundle ID User-visible notifications background background 5 bundle ID Silent refresh (content-available: 1) liveActivity liveactivity 5 bundleID.push-type.liveactivity Live Activity update/end (start deferred)

Content is keyed by kind — you send exactly one section (content.alert, content.background, or content.liveActivity) plus an optional kind-independent sealed blob the relay treats as opaque bytes (it is only size-checked, never decoded or logged).

docs.title: Enrollment in one paragraph
docs.text:
An app enrolls its device in three legs: POST /v1/enroll/begin sends a silent challenge push to the device (proving the token is real and reachable), POST /v1/enroll/finish proves the app is genuine via Apple App Attest and that the device received the challenge (assertion over SHA256(nonce ‖ serverChallenge)), and the relay returns a destination-bound grant plus a consent receipt. Renewal (POST /v1/enroll/renew) re-signs a grant with fresh credentials — no new attestation needed. Rotation (POST /v1/rotate) replaces a tenant's token and signing key as a pair — authorized by a signature under the current key — so paired devices re-enroll after a suspected key compromise. Revocation (POST /v1/revoke) denylists the grant's jti immediately.

Full contract: Enrollment spec v1.2.

docs.title: Why grants and signatures?
docs.text: A grant alone is not enough to push: /v1/push also requires the tenant token and a valid per-request Ed25519 signature over the body. So a leaked grant is useless without the tenant's credentials, and a leaked tenant token is useless without its signing key. Both are checked, every request, with ±5-minute timestamp skew and single-use nonces against replays.

docs.title: Limits & abuse
docs.text: Free to use, hostile to abuse: every lever is either automatic or one CLI command away.

docs.title: Automatic limits
docs.text:
Layer Limit Failure nginx (per IP, at the edge) limit_req burst/minute per route class 429 App quota — tenant burst quota.burst_per_min per minute 429 rate_limited App quota — per destination quota.token_burst_per_min per minute 429 token_rate_limited App quota — daily quota.daily per rolling 24h 429 quota_exhausted Register/enroll (per IP) 10/min per route class 429 rate_limited Request replay single-use nonce, 10-min window 401 replayed_nonce Clock skew ±5 minutes 401 stale_timestamp Tenant idle 30 days row deleted Unauthenticated body size 16 KiB (nginx) 413

All quota numbers are per App in operator config — there are no hidden global defaults. The relay charges quota before contacting APNs, so spamming the relay never becomes spamming Apple.

docs.title: Registration abuse
docs.text:
• /v1/register is rate-limited per IP, first-claim-wins (409 id_exists), and may require an HTTPS ownership callback (host must be the tenant id or a subdomain; DNS pinned to public addresses — the callback cannot probe private networks).
  • Callbacks are signed one-shot challenges, not webhooks: a third party can make the relay ping a URL it claims to own, at most the per-IP limit, and nothing else.

docs.title: Enrollment abuse
docs.text:
• The challenge push must be echoed by the device that owns the token (an attacker never receives it).
  • App Attest proves a genuine build of the app — chains to Apple's root, exact bundle ID, environment match.
  • User consent is collected in-app; the relay binds only what a human approved there (it stores no consent record — the receipt goes to the app).
  • Challenges are single-use and expire (default 10 minutes).

docs.title: Revocation levers (operator runbook)
docs.text:
# 1. Stop one grant immediately (tenant does this, or you do via denylist):
relay denylist add <jti> --expires 24h

# 2. Stop every destination for one token hash:
relay denylist add sha256:<hex> --expires 24h

# 3. Kill a tenant outright (their next request → 401 unknown_tenant):
relay tenant revoke <tenant-id>

# 4. Disable an App entirely: set `enabled: false` in config.yaml and
#    restart — pushes fail 403 app_disabled; new registrations get 400.

docs.title: Reporting abuse
docs.text:
If you host a public instance, publish an abuse contact in your instance's footer. For this project: open a GitHub issue (security-sensitive reports: use GitHub Security Advisories on the repo).

Operator responsibility

A relay operator is the controller of the little data that exists (token digests, blind indexes). The privacy page is the contract to your tenants — keep it true for your deployment.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: The relay is built so that running it tells an operator as little as possible about anyone's business — including theirs.

docs.title: What is stored (the complete list)
docs.text: Table Contents tenants tenant id, App id, token digest, Ed25519 public key, timestamps usage timestamps bucketed per tenant/day and per blind index nonces SHA-256 of used nonces (replay window, 10 minutes) challenges challenge id, App, tenant id, token digest, nonces, expiry denylist grant jti or sha256:… token hash + expiry

docs.title: What the relay never sees (by construction)
docs.text:
• Destination tokens in the clear, at rest. A push request's destinationToken is used to address APNs and to HMAC into a blind index (HMAC(master_secret, token)) for quota buckets, then discarded. Without the operator-held master secret the index cannot be reversed or linked back across days even if the database leaks.
  • Payload content. Content is validated against per-App caps, encoded, and forwarded; nothing is logged or retained. sealed content is decrypted by you, never by the relay — it only checks its size.
  • Who your users are. There is no device table, no session table, no user identity. The relay knows "some tenant sent a push to a bucket" — nothing more.
  • Grants, once. Grants are verified statelessly and only remembered if you revoke one (jti on the denylist).
  • Anything in logs. Events carry route, status, machine error code and latency. Tokens, grants, payloads and tenant ids never appear in output from relay logs or relay metrics.

docs.title: Third parties
docs.text:
• APNs sees what any APNs sender sees: the token you address, your (operator's) app topic, and the payload — that is Apple's platform, not the relay's doing.
  • GitHub hosts the docs/site (Pages) and the source; the repository is public and contains no secrets (.p8, config.yaml, .env, relay.db are gitignored).

docs.title: Retention & deletion
docs.text:
• 30-day non-use deletion: a tenant row that has not been used for 30 days is deleted entirely — token digest, public key, all of it. The next authenticated call returns 401 unknown_tenant; re-registration starts clean.
  • Operator kill switch: relay tenant revoke <id> deletes immediately; the next request fails with unknown_tenant.
  • Rate-limit state ages out in minutes; usage rows in 24 hours; nonces in 10 minutes; challenges at expiry (≤1 hour).
  • Backups (if the operator makes them) inherit all of the above — the schema is the privacy boundary; there is nothing else in the file.

docs.title: Self-hosting
docs.text: The relay ships as a container image (ghcr.io/timlaing/apns-push-relay, one tag per release) and runs as a Docker Compose stack: nginx (TLS + rate limits), certbot (automatic renewal), and the relay (FastAPI + SQLite). Building from source is supported, but not required — the image is the primary path.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A host with a public IP, ports 80/443 open, and DNS A/AAAA records for your API and docs domains.
  • Apple side: an APNs authentication key (.p8, Key ID, Team ID) per App you relay for — created under Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles → Keys with the Apple Push Notifications service (APNs) capability enabled (an App Store Connect API key is a different thing and APNs rejects it) — plus the App Attestation root certificates (see below).
  • Docker with the Compose plugin.

docs.title: 2. Configure
docs.text:
The compose file, nginx template and config examples live in the repo — clone it (or copy deploy/ onto your host):

git clone https://github.com/timlaing/apns-push-relay.git
cd apns-push-relay
cp deploy/config.yaml.example deploy/config.yaml
cp deploy/.env.example deploy/.env

.env — your domains and two secrets; nothing domain-related is hardcoded anywhere. The values in .env.example are placeholders — replace them. Secrets must be ≥32 characters; .env is gitignored:

API_DOMAIN=…            # this instance's API hostname (A record → VPS)
LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL=…     # certbot sends expiry notices here
RELAY_ADMIN_TOKEN=…     # powers `relay` / the admin API
RELAY_MASTER_SECRET=…   # HMAC key for blind destination indexes

.env drives nginx and certbot; the server: block in config.yaml below holds the relay's own options (swagger_ui).

deploy/config.yaml — everything structural lives here; nothing is hardcoded in the code. Relative paths (keys/…) resolve against the config file's directory — deploy/ on the host, /etc/apns-relay/ in the container (compose mounts ./keys there):

server:
  swagger_ui: false # true → Swagger UI at /docs, ReDoc, OpenAPI schema

enrollment:
  grant_issuer_key: keys/issuer.pem # Ed25519 (see below)
  challenge_ttl: 600
  # App Attest root: downloaded automatically at container startup and
  # verified against a pinned SHA-256 (see below). Override the URL or the
  # paths to manage the file yourself.
  attest_root_url: https://www.apple.com/certificateauthority/Apple_App_Attestation_Root_CA.pem
  attest_root_certs:
    development: /var/lib/apns-relay/apple-attest-root.pem
    production: /var/lib/apns-relay/apple-attest-root.pem

storage:
  database: /var/lib/apns-relay/relay.db

apps:
  - id: my-app
    display_name: My App
    bundle_id: com.example.myapp
    team_id: ABCDEFGHIJ
    key_id: XXXXXXXXXX # 10-char id from the AuthKey_<KEYID>.p8 filename
    environments: [production]
    kinds: [alert, background, liveActivity]
    live_activity: true
    attest_environment: production
    quota: { burst_per_min: 60, daily: 10000, token_burst_per_min: 30 }
    grant_ttl: { min: 900, max: 86400, default: 21600 }
    caps: { title: 64, body: 200, sealed: 1024, background: 512 }

Generate the grant-issuer key once:

mkdir -p deploy/keys
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out deploy/keys/issuer.pem

Name every .p8 AuthKey_<KEYID>.p8 and drop it in deploy/keys/; set that app's key_id to the 10-character id — the relay looks the file up at keys/AuthKey_<key_id>.p8 next to the config file. Keep it all outside the repo (the gitignore excludes keys/, *.p8, config.yaml, .env and the database).

docs.title: 3. Validate before starting
docs.text:
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm relay relay doctor --offline

relay doctor --offline checks the local files: config schema, every .p8 (P-256 parse + JWT pre-signature), the issuer key (Ed25519), App Attest roots, RELAY_MASTER_SECRET, and database writability. The container entrypoint runs the same check on every start — a broken deploy fails fast instead of at the first push. Once the stack is up, relay doctor (without --offline) runs the same checks through the admin API, against the running server itself.

docs.title: 4. Up, and TLS
docs.text:
Pull the published relay image, build the local nginx edge image (it adds openssl for the first-boot placeholder certificate), and start — no build toolchain needed beyond Docker:

docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml pull relay
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml build nginx
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d

Building from source (alternative)

To run a modified build — or when no release image exists yet — let compose build from the checkout instead (build: in docker-compose.yml; up --build rebuilds everything):

docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d --build

certbot obtains certificates via the ACME webroot nginx exposes, and renews on a timer; nginx reloads after renewal. Verify:

curl -sS https://api.push.example.org/health        # {"status": "ok"}
docker compose exec relay relay status

Staging first

Use Let's Encrypt staging while iterating on DNS to avoid rate limits — the compose file documents the switch.

Behind another proxy

If this stack sits behind an existing TLS-terminating proxy (an ingress, another nginx, a tunnel), set FORCE_HTTPS=0 in .env and recreate the stack: port 80 then serves requests arriving with X-Forwarded-Proto: https instead of redirecting them. The certbot service is scaled to zero in this mode — no ACME client or renewal loop runs, and LETSENCRYPT_EMAIL is only required when it runs. Plain port-80 requests still redirect, and /admin still 404s at the edge. Forward the original Host header from the upstream proxy, and have it overwrite or append the real client address in X-Forwarded-For — in this mode nginx passes that list through untouched, and per-IP rate limiting keys on its last entry.

docs.title: 5. Day-two operations
docs.text:
docker compose exec relay relay status              # version + health + quota + metrics
docker compose exec relay relay version             # package version
docker compose exec relay relay monitor --interval 5   # live dashboard (status, quotas, recent requests)
docker compose exec relay relay logs --errors --since 1h
docker compose exec relay relay tenant list
docker compose exec relay relay tenant revoke hooks.example.com   # kill switch
docker compose exec relay relay denylist add <jti|sha256:…> --expires 24h
docker compose exec relay relay metrics             # metric table (--json / --prom too)
  • The relay process serves two listeners: the public API on port 8001 (nginx's upstream, bound to host loopback for pre-nginx CLI/Swagger) and the admin API on its own port 8000 (host loopback only, the CLI's default target). The public listener has no /admin routes at all, and nginx returns 404 for /admin.

  • Adding or removing apps: relay app add (interactively picks from the server's keys/AuthKey_*.p8) and relay app remove go through the admin API — the relay process edits config.yaml, preserving comments and writing a .bak. Run them inside the container (docker compose exec relay relay app add; the CLI only makes API calls, so no elevated user is needed) and then docker compose restart relay (config is loaded at boot; the entrypoint re-runs the offline doctor on every start). From the host, export RELAY_ADMIN_TOKEN and point RELAY_API_URL at http://127.0.0.1:8000 to drive the same commands.

  • Remote CLI without the checkout: install straight from the repo with uv tool install git+https://github.com/timlaing/apns-push-relay. Keep the admin API on host loopback and reach it through an SSH tunnel (ssh -fN -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 <relay-host> — backgrounded, so no remote shell opens), then export RELAY_ADMIN_TOKEN and use the default RELAY_API_URL (http://127.0.0.1:8000) — never expose port 8000 itself.

  • Interactive API docs: set swagger_ui: true under server: in config.yaml to serve Swagger UI at /docs, ReDoc at /redoc and the schema at /openapi.json on the API domain (off by default — the published schema lives on the docs site either way).
  • Tenant credentials are tenant-side: a tenant rotates its own token and signing key with POST /v1/rotate (signed under the current key). Operator kill switches stay relay tenant revoke (kill) and relay tenant reissue (new token, key untouched).
  • Back up relay.db (named volume) — it is the only state; it contains digests and blind indexes, never raw tokens or payloads.
  • Upgrades: git pull && docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml pull relay && … up -d for the image path (or … up -d --build on a source build); pull relay tracks latest — GHCR also publishes per-version and sha tags if you prefer to pin. Doctor pre-flight gates the swap.

docs.title: App Attest roots
docs.text:
Apple publishes a single App Attestation Root CA — development and production attestations chain to it and are separated by AAGUID (spec §2.2) — at a public link on Apple's certificate-authority page (no Apple Developer sign-in needed). The container downloads it at startup into /var/lib/apns-relay/apple-attest-root.pem and verifies it against a pinned SHA-256 fingerprint: a tampered response or an Apple rotation fails loudly rather than trusting the download. To re-download or update it later:

docker compose exec relay relay doctor --fetch-roots    # re-download + full checks
docker compose exec relay relay fetch-roots --if-missing  # the startup step, rerun by hand

Set enrollment.attest_root_url: null to manage the file(s) entirely yourself — point enrollment.attest_root_certs at your own PEMs; relay doctor validates whichever files are configured (subject, expiry with a warning under 90 days, fingerprint) either way. Until a root for an App's attest_environment resolves the relay fails closed: enroll/finish returns 400 attestation_unavailable and no grants are issued — pushes of already-valid grants are unaffected. The startup download is best-effort: an offline boot still serves.

docs.text:

docs.title: Probe it yourself
docs.text:
curl -sS https://api.push.example.org/health
curl -sS https://api.push.example.org/metrics | head

/metrics is a Prometheus text snapshot of request counts, APNs result counts (accepted/invalidDestination/retryable/rejected), auth failure codes and tenant expiry counts — aggregate only, no identifiers.

docs.title: Enrollment & Grant Specification + Threat Model
docs.text:
Status: Reviewed v1.0 — M0 gate complete (19 October 2026); amended v1.1 — attestation binding steps, signing-key TOFU, Live Activity events (see §7); amended v1.2 — credential rotation (§2.7, see §7)

Version: 1.2 · 19 October 2026

Applies to: relay protocol version 1

License: MIT · Copyright (c) 2026 Tim Laing

This document specifies the highest-risk part of the relay: how a device becomes authorized to receive pushes for a tenant, and how that authorization is represented, renewed, and revoked. It was written and reviewed before any code was written, per the originating design requirements ("specify and review the enrollment challenge/attestation mechanism… Do not claim a fully secure, stateless enrollment protocol has already been verified"). Review outcomes are recorded in §6; the four open questions from the draft are now decisions.

Everything here is protocol version 1. Breaking changes require a new version segment in grant encoding and endpoint paths.

docs.title: 1. Roles and trust model
docs.text:
Party Holds Trusted for Relay operator .p8 keys, grant-issuer signing key, config Correct key custody; not trusted with sealed content (by design) Tenant backend Tenant token, tenant Ed25519 keypair, grants Nothing beyond its own users' devices iOS app Device token, App Attest key, user consent Being the sole consent authority; genuine-build proof Apple APNs, App Attest roots Platform root of trust (unavoidable)

Authorization for one push requires three independent proofs:

  1. Genuine app — App Attest (the relay will only bind devices running a real, operator-configured build).
  2. Destination possession — an APNs challenge push the device must echo (the relay will only bind a token the requester actually holds).
  3. User consent — the enrollment runs inside the app after an explicit consent step (the relay binds only what a human approved).

No single proof suffices: attestation alone doesn't prove token ownership; possession alone could be a cloned client; neither implies user intent.

docs.title: Trust limitation stated honestly
docs.text:
The operator of an instance holds the .p8 and grant-issuer key, but that alone does not let them push to enrolled devices: APNs requires a destination device token, and the relay never stores one — tokens exist only transiently in enroll/begin and /v1/push requests, and only their SHA-256 hashes are persisted (challenge rows, grants). The stock relay therefore cannot push to a device it has never been asked to reach, and cannot re-reach one whose token it saw only in passing once that request is over.

The residual risk is a modified build: an operator willing to alter the code could log tokens as they transit and mint grants for them. That is the real trust boundary — tenants trust that the operator runs the published software, not a doctored variant. Mitigations: sealed content keeps tenant message detail blind even to a logging operator; no-storage limits knowledge to what actively transits; self-hosting removes the third party entirely. Optional future hardening (not v1): published image digests or reproducible builds so tenants can verify the relay runs unmodified code. This belongs in docs/privacy.md verbatim.

docs.title: 2. Enrollment flow
docs.text:
iOS app (genuine, user consented)              Relay                    APNs
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼───
 1. app: user taps "Enable remote alerts for <backend>"
 2. app ── POST /v1/enroll/begin ───────────────►│
      { app, tenantId, destinationToken }        │
      (tenantId + tenant pubkey come from the    │  validate app exists & kind
       paired backend; destinationToken is the   │  allowed; token format ok;
       fresh APNs token)                         │  mint serverChallenge (1-use,
                                                 │  10-min TTL)
 3.                                                 ├─ silent APNs push ────► device
      challenge payload: { challengeId, nonce } ◄───┘  (content-available)
 4. app: DCAppAttestService.prepare(serverChallenge)
     app: attestKey(keyId, SHA256(serverChallenge))          → attestation
     app: fetchAssertion(keyId, SHA256(nonce ‖ serverChallenge)) → assertion
 5. app ── POST /v1/enroll/finish ─────────────►│
      { challengeId, attestation, assertion,    │  verify challengeId+nonce
        tenantId, tenantPubkey, kinds }         │  verify attestation chain +
                                                 │  app ID + environment
                                                 │  verify assertion signature
                                                 │  issue grant (Ed25519)
 6. grant returned to app
 7. app ── grant over paired TLS connection ──► tenant backend
                                                 (app↔backend channel; relay
                                                  never contacts the backend)

Foreground requirement: step 3 is a silent (background) push, which iOS throttles. Enrollment therefore requires the app to be active in the foreground — which it is, because the user just tapped consent. The contract must state this; silent push is used as a possession challenge, not as a reliable wake-up mechanism.

docs.title: 2.1 POST /v1/enroll/begin (unauthenticated, rate-limited per IP)
docs.text:
{
  "app": "my-app",
  "tenantId": "hooks.example.com",
  "destinationToken": "<APNs device or ActivityKit token>"
}
  • app must exist and permit the requested operation; destinationToken format-validated (length/charset), never stored — only used to send the challenge and hashed into the grant.
  • Response: { "challengeId": "<uuid>", "serverChallenge": "<32B b64u>", "expiresAt": <epoch+600> }.
  • If the challenge push fails at APNs (410, invalid token) → 400 invalidDestination; nothing is stored.
  • State: one row (challengeId, app, tenantId, token hash, nonce, serverChallenge, expiry). Deleted on use or expiry. This is the only enrollment state; it is separate from the stateless delivery path.

docs.title: 2.2 POST /v1/enroll/finish (unauthenticated, rate-limited per IP)
docs.text:
{
  "challengeId": "<uuid>",
  "attestation": "<base64 Apple attestation>",
  "assertion": "<base64 Apple assertion>",
  "tenantId": "hooks.example.com",
  "tenantPubkey": "<Ed25519 public key, base64>",
  "kinds": ["alert", "liveActivity"],
  "ttl": 21600
}
  • ttl optional — requested grant lifetime in seconds; clamped to the App's grant_ttl bounds (§2.5). Omitted → App default.

Response (grant + machine-readable consent receipt):

{
  "grant": "v1.<claims>.<sig>",
  "consent": {
    "tenant": "hooks.example.com",
    "app": "my-app",
    "appDisplayName": "My App",
    "kinds": ["alert", "liveActivity"],
    "boundAt": 1792230900,
    "expiresAt": 1792252500,
    "environment": "production"
  }
}

The consent object is informational JSON describing exactly what was bound and for how long — returned so the app can decide what to do with it (display in settings, log locally, discard). The relay stores none of it; it is derived from the grant that was just issued.

Verification, all mandatory:

  1. challengeId exists, unexpired, unused; request tenantId matches.
  2. The pushed nonce must be bound into the assertion's signed data (SHA256(nonce ‖ serverChallenge)) — possession proof, single-use.
  3. App Attest — verify, in order (Apple, "Validating apps that connect to your server"):
  4. the x5c chain to Apple's App Attestation Root, and leaf validity dates;
  5. the nonce extension (OID 1.2.840.113635.100.8.2) inside the leaf certificate equals SHA256(authData ‖ SHA256(nonce ‖ serverChallenge)) — this is what binds the Apple-signed certificate to the otherwise unsigned authData;
  6. the credential ID equals SHA256(leaf public key) in X9.62 uncompressed point form, and the COSE key inside authData hashes to the same value (the attested key pair and the certified key are one);
  7. the attested app ID equals the configured bundle ID (rpIdHash) — for assertions too;
  8. authData.counter is 0 in the attestation (counters advance only in assertions);
  9. the AAGUID matches the App's attest_environment (appattestdevelop for development, appattest + seven zero bytes for production). Extract the credential public key.
  10. Verify the assertion signature with that credential key over SHA256(nonce ‖ serverChallenge), re-checking the assertion's rpIdHash against the configured bundle ID.
  11. kinds ⊆ the App's configured allowed kinds.
  12. Signing key is trust-on-first-use. tenantPubkey is stored only while the tenant has no key; a different key for an already-bound tenant is rejected (invalid_pubkey) — enroll/finish is unauthenticated by design, so key replacement would let anyone holding a stolen token impersonate the tenant. The only way to change a bound key is authenticated POST /v1/rotate (§2.7), which verifies a signature under the current key first. relay tenant revoke remains the revocation control (§2.6).

Failure at any step → 400, challenge burned (single-use even on failure after nonce consumption). Success → challenge row deleted, grant issued.

Implementation note (M4): follow Apple's current App Attest verification document for exact CBOR field handling and root-cert distribution; this spec fixes the security properties (chain, nonce-extension binding, credential-ID binding, app ID, environment/AAGUID, single-use serverChallenge, nonce binding, signing-key TOFU), not Apple's wire encoding. Validate against a physical device before enabling for any production App.

docs.title: 2.3 Grant format
docs.text:
grant = "v1." ‖ b64u(claims) ‖ "." ‖ b64u(Ed25519_sig(claims))
claims = canonical JSON (sorted keys, no whitespace):
{ "jti":   "<uuid>",                     // denylist handle; rotates on renewal
  "iss":   "<grant-issuer key id>",      // single issuer key in v1
  "tok":   "sha256:…",                  // SHA-256 of destination token
  "ten":   "hooks.example.com",       // tenant ID
  "tpk":   "<tenant pubkey, base64>",    // binding — see note
  "app":   "my-app",
  "kinds": ["alert", "background", "liveActivity"],
  "env":   "production",                 // from app config, not the caller
  "iat":   1792230900,
  "exp":   1792252500,                   // iat + ttl (§2.5)
  "ttl":   21600 }                       // effective grant TTL, seconds
  • Topic and APNs environment are never caller-supplied — resolved from app via operator config.
  • Verification is database-free: signature → issuer key, exp, denylist, tok vs the token presented in the push request, ten/tpk vs the authenticated tenant, kinds vs the requested kind.
  • tpk binds the grant to the tenant's signing key: presenting another tenant's keypair fails request authentication regardless of the grant.
  • A stolen grant alone cannot push: /v1/push also requires the tenant token and a valid Ed25519 request signature. Grants are bearer-ish only in combination with tenant credentials.
  • Transport: returned in the enroll/finish response; the app delivers it to its backend over the existing paired TLS connection. The relay never contacts the backend and stores nothing about the grant beyond the jti denylist entry created on revocation.

docs.title: 2.4 POST /v1/enroll/renew (tenant-authenticated, signed)
docs.text:
• Requires tenant token + canonical Ed25519 request signature (token-bound, as /v1/push) and the current grant.
  • Verified like /v1/push plus: grant unexpired, jti not denylisted, tenant matches. New grant issued with new jti, iat = now, exp = now + ttl, where ttl is the requested value clamped to App bounds (§2.5; omitted → App default); all other claims unchanged. Old grant lapses naturally at its exp (no backdating, no lifetime extension beyond one TTL per renewal).
  • Renewal is authenticated possession of tenant credentials — no new App Attest or challenge push: the destination binding was proven at enrollment and the token hash cannot change without re-enrollment.

docs.title: 2.5 Grant lifetime — App-bounded, tenant-configured
docs.text:
Per-App config sets the bounds; the tenant chooses its own TTL within them (requested at enroll/finish and again at each renew; omitted → App default):

grant_ttl: { min: 900, max: 86400, default: 21600 } # seconds; min 15m, max 24h
  • Operator keeps the abuse ceiling (max) and floor (min); a tenant that wants 10-minute grants for tight revocation semantics or 24-hour grants for an unattended home server can have either, and anything between.
  • Requested TTL outside bounds → clamped to the nearest bound (documented behavior, not an error — avoids brittle clients).
  • Renewal may change the TTL (within the same bounds) — the new exp is now + requested_ttl.
  • Rationale unchanged: short enough that a leaked grant (including tpk) is inert quickly, long enough that a backend outage of reasonable length doesn't mass-invalidate deliveries. Renewal is cheap; schedule at ≤ ½ TTL.

docs.title: 2.6 Revocation
docs.text:
Path Trigger Effect POST /v1/revoke (tenant-authed, signed) Backend unsubscribes a device jti denylisted until its natural exp (bounded storage) Operator CLI relay denylist add Abuse response jti, tenant, or token-hash denylisted; tenant-wide kill supported 30-day non-use deletion Inactivity Tenant + all grants' jtis implicitly dead (tenant token no longer validates) Re-enrollment New token / new consent Old grant simply lapses; new grant issued for the same key (TOFU, §2.2 step 6). A different key requires POST /v1/rotate (§2.7) or relay tenant revoke + re-registration

Denylist entries carry the grant's exp as their natural purge time — no unbounded growth. There is no per-grant stateful check on the delivery path: verification reads the denylist (small, hot) and nothing else.

docs.title: 2.7 POST /v1/rotate (tenant-authenticated, signed) — credential rotation
docs.text:
• Request: {"pubkey": "<replacement Ed25519 pubkey, base64url>"}
  • Auth: tenant token + canonical Ed25519 request signature (token-bound, as /v1/push) under the current binding
  • Response: 200 {"tenant", "app", "token", "rotated_at"} — token is shown once, like register

The two credentials age differently: an operator can reissue the token (relay tenant reissue), but until §2.7 the tenant could not replace its own signing key. A signed request under the current keypair is exactly proof of possession, so rotation lives on the authenticated route — never on unauthenticated enroll/finish (§2.2 step 6).

Semantics:

  • Verification runs before anything changes: a stale keypair gets 401 invalid_signature, a stale token 401 unknown_tenant, an unenrolled registration 401 enrollment_required.
  • Token digest and stored pubkey are replaced in one write; the old token stops verifying immediately. Sending the current pubkey is a token-only rotation (key untouched).
  • Outstanding grants carry the old key (tpk) and stop verifying: 403 tenant_mismatch on /v1/push, 403 grant_mismatch on renew. Devices re-enroll with the replacement key — TOFU passes because the stored key is the one being enrolled (§2.2 step 6).
  • Tenant id, App, quotas and last_seen continue unchanged; the nonce and skew rules of the signed-request contract apply as to every signed route.

Threat posture: an attacker who already holds both token and keypair can act as the tenant (A7) and can likewise rotate — rotation is the tenant's incident response: rotate once, re-enroll devices, and the old key stops verifying everywhere at once.

docs.title: 3.1 Assets
docs.text: .p8 keys · grant-issuer key · tenant tokens + keypairs · device tokens · notification content (plaintext fields + sealed blob) · user attention (banners are a resource) · Apple account reputation (APNs abuse → throttling or key revocation).

docs.title: 3.2 Adversaries and mitigations
docs.text: # Attack Mitigation A1 Replay a captured push request TLS + single-use nonce + token-bound canonical signature (PLAN §3.2) A2 Splice a stolen signature onto another tenant's token Token digest inside the signed message; verification binds them A3 Enroll a victim's device token (unsolicited pushes) Challenge push must be echoed — attacker never receives it; App Attest requires a genuine app; user consent required in-app A4 Cloned/fake client enrolling devices App Attest chain + nonce-extension / credential-ID binding + exact bundle-ID + AAGUID/environment check; no attestation → no grant A5 Use a stolen grant to push Grant alone is insufficient (tenant token + signature also required); short TTL; jti denylist; token-hash binding stops token substitution A6 Stolen tenant token without keypair Cannot sign requests → 401; relay tenant reissue rotates A7 Stolen tenant token and keypair Full tenant impersonation until detected — bounded by per-key quotas, per-token caps, denylist, 30-day expiry; incident path is relay denylist add --tenant A8 SSRF / internal probing via callback PublicHTTPS guard: HTTPS/443 only, resolve-once, global-address-only, TLS pinned A9 Quota exhaustion / spam one device Per-App burst/daily quota, per-token blind-index cap, nginx per-IP limit_req, 16 KB body cap A10 Push arbitrary topic / environment / APNs host Never caller-supplied; resolved from app in operator config A11 Phishing banners under a trusted app's name Structured capped fields only (no raw APNs payload), operator-revocable, documented content policy A12 Device token or content leak from relay storage No device table, no payload persistence, no content in logs; tokens hashed where stored at all A13 Malicious relay operator (modified build logging tokens in transit) Tokens never stored by the stock relay — nothing to steal at rest; sealed blob keeps detail blind; honest disclosure (§1); self-hosting removes the party; optional future: verifiable image digests A14 Enrollment-endpoint DoS Per-IP rate limits on enroll/*, challenge TTL, single-use rows A15 Grant-issuer key compromise Single issuer key in v1 (no key-set shipping). Rotation runbook (M8): install new key, restart — all outstanding grants (≤ max 24h TTL) lapse early; tenants re-enroll. iss claim present from v1 so a key set can be added later without a grant-format break A16 Replace a tenant's signing key via unauthenticated enroll/finish Signing key is trust-on-first-use (§2.2 step 6): stored only while empty; a different key → invalid_pubkey; concurrent first-enroll writes are conditional. Rotation only via authenticated POST /v1/rotate (§2.7): a signature under the current key proves possession before replacement; relay tenant revoke stays the revocation control

docs.title: 3.3 Out of scope (v1)
docs.text:
• Compromise of the device itself or its keychain.
  • Apple/platform failures (APNs outage, App Attest outage) — surfaced as retryable / enrollment failure, never silently.
  • Exactly-once delivery (APNs does not provide it; tenants own retry policy).
  • Push-to-start Live Activities (deferred).

docs.title: 4. Known limitations (published in docs, not hidden here)
docs.text:
1. Operator trust — §1: holding the keys is not sufficient — device tokens are never stored, so an operator can only target devices whose tokens actively transit a modified relay. Trust reduces to "the operator runs the published software"; sealed content, no-storage, and self-hosting are the mitigations.
  2. Silent-push challenge — enrollment needs the app foregrounded; a throttled challenge push fails the flow cleanly (retry begin).
  3. No instant revocation of a grant without its jti known — revocation is by jti (known to the holder and, on revoke, to the relay); a grant leaked without any handle lives only to its short exp.
  4. App reinstall / token rotation — new token ⇒ tok mismatch ⇒ invalidDestination ⇒ re-enrollment. Correct but requires app-side detection and a user-visible retry.
  5. Attestation replay across devices — an assertion is bound to one device's credential key and one serverChallenge; cross-device replay fails signature verification. Server-challenge freshness bounds the window.

docs.title: 5. Test requirements (M4 gate, distilled from PLAN §13)
docs.text:
• Enrollment rejects: bad attestation chain, wrong app ID, wrong environment, reused challengeId, wrong/expired nonce, kinds not allowed, unknown tenant.
  • Forged/expired/cross-destination/cross-tenant grants rejected; tok substitution rejected; denylist effective within one request.
  • Renewal: unexpired grant only, jti rotates, old grant lapses at exp.
  • Physical-device end-to-end: consent → enroll → alert, Live Activity update/end, and sandbox/production separation verified.
  • No secrets, tokens, nonces, or attestation blobs in logs.

docs.title: 6. Review decisions (recorded 19 Oct 2026)
docs.text:
The four M0 open questions are resolved:

  1. Grant TTL — tenant-configurable within App bounds. Per-App config sets grant_ttl: {min, max, default} (bounds 15 min–24 h); the tenant requests a ttl at enroll/finish and may change it at each renew. Out-of-bounds is clamped, not rejected. Operator keeps the abuse ceiling. (§2.2, §2.4, §2.5)
  2. Consent receipt — yes, as JSON, app's discretion. enroll/finish returns a machine-readable consent object (tenant, app, kinds, boundAt, expiresAt, environment). The relay stores none of it; the app decides what to do (display, log, discard). (§2.2)
  3. Issuer keys — do not ship key support. v1 uses a single grant-issuer key. Rotation is an M8 runbook: install new key, restart, outstanding grants (≤ max TTL) lapse early, tenants re-enroll. The iss claim is present from v1 so a key set can be introduced later without a grant-format break. (A15)
  4. ActivityKit tokens — same enrollment flow. kind: liveActivity with the activity push token as destinationToken; no separate channel. The destination-token hash makes alert and liveActivity bindings naturally disjoint, and App Attest / challenge-push / consent apply identically. (§2.1)

docs.title: 7. Amendments (v1.1–v1.2, 19 October 2026)
docs.text:
Recorded here so the reviewed v1.0 text and the implemented behavior stay traceable. Items 1–4 came out of the post-implementation review; item 5 records the v1.2 addition. None weaken a v1.0 property.

  1. Attestation binding steps made explicit (§2.2 step 3). v1.0 named the security properties (chain, app ID, environment); v1.1 pins the exact Apple verification steps that realize them — the leaf-certificate nonce extension (1.2.840.113635.100.8.2 = SHA256(authData ‖ SHA256(nonce ‖ serverChallenge))), credential-ID = SHA256(leaf public key) (X9.62 uncompressed), COSE key hash equality, attestation counter 0, and AAGUID pinned per attest_environment. Without the nonce extension check, authData (unsigned) could be forged alongside a replayed genuine chain — voiding threat A4.
  2. Assertion rpIdHash re-check (§2.2 step 4). Apple's assertion verification includes re-validating the app-ID hash in the assertion's own authenticator data.
  3. Signing key is trust-on-first-use (§2.2 step 6, threat A16). enroll/finish is unauthenticated by design, so a stored tenantPubkey can never be replaced through it. relay tenant revoke is a revocation control, not a rotation mechanism — there is no key rotation in v1; a revoked tenant re-registers as a new binding.
  4. Live Activity events are update/end only. Push-to-start requires attributes-type/attributes, which this API does not carry; start is rejected rather than accepted-and-dropped (PLAN §1 already deferred it).
  5. Credential rotation added (§2.7, v1.2). Supersedes the "no key rotation" note in amendment 3: POST /v1/rotate now exists, but only on the authenticated route — a signature under the current binding is the possession proof, and both token and pubkey are replaced in one write. enroll/finish stays TOFU-conditional (§2.2 step 6); relay tenant revoke stays a revocation control (§2.6).

docs.title: OpenAPI reference
docs.text: Machine-readable schema for every endpoint, generated from the running code by scripts/export_openapi.py — regenerate it whenever routes change (uv run python scripts/export_openapi.py).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Base URL: your instance's API host — API_DOMAIN in .env (e.g. https://api.push.example.org).
  • Content type: application/json everywhere; unknown request fields are rejected (422 invalid_request, extra="forbid").
  • Signed routes — /v1/push, /v1/enroll/renew, /v1/revoke, /v1/rotate — carry Authorization: Bearer tnt_…, X-Relay-Time, X-Relay-Nonce, X-Relay-Signature (canonical message in Getting started).
  • Push results are always 200 with result ∈ {accepted, invalidDestination, retryable, rejected}.
  • Error envelope: {"error": "<machine-code>", "detail": "<optional>"}.
  • The admin API (/admin/*) is not in this schema — it is internal, never proxied by nginx, and authenticated by RELAY_ADMIN_TOKEN.
  • Interactive docs: an instance can serve this schema as Swagger UI at /docs (plus ReDoc at /redoc and raw /openapi.json) when the operator sets server.swagger_ui: true — off by default.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method & path Auth Purpose POST /v1/register — Tenant token issuance (per App, once) POST /v1/push signed Deliver one push against a grant POST /v1/enroll/begin — Challenge push for a destination token POST /v1/enroll/finish — App Attest + assertion → grant + consent POST /v1/enroll/renew signed Fresh grant, new jti, same bindings POST /v1/revoke signed Denylist a grant's jti POST /v1/rotate signed Rotate tenant token + signing key

Regenerating
